On a connected compact Hermitian manifold (M,ω), for nonnegative F∈L^r(M,ω^d), r>1, with positive integral, any two continuous ω-psh solutions of (ω+Dφ)^d=cFω^d with positive coefficients have the same coefficient c, where D=i∂bar∂/π. [Nguyen, Corollary 0.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.00891v1).

Let (M,ω) be a connected compact Kähler manifold of positive complex dimension d with ∫_Mω^d=1, and let µ be a positive Radon probability. There exists a canonical ω-psh φ whose actual non-pluripolar measure µ_φ equals µ and has mass one if and only if µ charges no pluripolar set. Here D=i∂bar∂/π, µ_φ=lim_j 1_{φ>−j}(ω+D max(φ,−j))^d, and E(M,ω) is defined by µ_φ(M)=1. [Guedj–Zeriahi, Definition 1.1 and Theorem 4.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0612630v2).

On a compact complex manifold M, a smooth real (1,1)-form θ, without a closedness assumption, admits a real distribution ψ with θ+dd^cψ≥0 whenever ∫_Mθ∧T≥0 for every smooth strictly positive real (d−1,d−1)-form T satisfying dd^cT=0. The assertion is invariant under positive rescaling of dd^c. [Lamari, Lemma 3.3](https://www.numdam.org/article/AIF_1999__49_1_263_0.pdf).

On an open Ω⊂C^d, every real distribution with positive complex Hessian has a unique locally integrable canonical psh representative. The locally integrable psh cone is closed in L^1_loc, and its subsets bounded in L^1 on every compact subset are relatively compact in L^1_loc. For a nonempty family of psh functions locally uniformly bounded above, its upper-regularized supremum is psh and equals the raw supremum almost everywhere. [Demailly, I.5.7–5.9](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~demarco/Math274/Demailly_ComplexAnalyticDiffGeom.pdf).

For a d-closed positive current T of bidimension (p,p) on a complex manifold and every c>0, the geometric Lelong upperlevel set {x:ν(T,x)≥c} is analytic and has complex dimension at most p. [Siu’s theorem, Demailly III.8.5](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~demarco/Math274/Demailly_ComplexAnalyticDiffGeom.pdf).

On a connected compact Hermitian manifold (M,ω) of complex dimension d≥2, every smooth real F admits a unique real b and a unique smooth real φ with sup_Mφ=0 satisfying ω+i∂bar∂φ>0 and (ω+i∂bar∂φ)^d=e^(F+b)ω^d. [Tosatti–Weinkove, Corollary 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0910.1390v2).

The specified primary PDFs were inspected:

• Kolodziej–Nguyen, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.5491v2, PDF page 1, Theorem 0.1: continuous admissible potentials and positive normalization scalars exist for nonnegative L^p densities, p>1, with positive integral. Zeros are allowed, and no lower-volume hypothesis appears.
• Nguyen, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.00891v1, PDF page 2, Corollary 0.2, proved as Corollary 2.7 on pages 16–17: the scalar of any continuous constant-normalization equation is identified by exponential normalizations and is uniquely determined. This does not supply unbounded-potential uniqueness.
• Guedj–Zeriahi, https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0612630v2, Theorem A on page 2 and Theorem 4.6 on page 26: a measure with background total volume and no pluripolar charge has a solution in E. The introduction permits every positive complex dimension. Definition 1.1 on page 3 defines E by actual full mass of the finite-truncation measure. Thus k=2 is covered.

These statements are explicitly permitted external inputs. This note checks their premises and conventions, rather than independently proving the external existence theorems.

Write δ=i∂bar∂/(2π) for the task operator. All three papers use D=i∂bar∂/π=2δ; GZ defines d^c=(∂−bar∂)/(2iπ). If w is a source potential, set v=2w. Then η+δv=η+Dw for the same background η, preserving the equation and scalar. For singular potentials,

max(2w,−j)=2max(w,−j/2), and {2w>−j}={w>−j/2}.

The finite-level measures consequently agree at corresponding levels. Integer and half-integer levels are cofinal in the defining increasing limit, so the actual extended measure and full mass are preserved. The exponential parameter is halved when expressed in task potentials; scalar uniqueness is unaffected.

For a nonzero nonnegative g∈L¹(κ^k), let G=∫gκ^k and ν=(g/G)κ^k. This is a probability measure without pluripolar charge. Indeed, locally a pluripolar set lies in the −∞ locus of a nonidentically infinite psh function; local integrability makes that locus Lebesgue-null. A countable coordinate cover gives smooth-volume measure zero, and absolute continuity gives ν-measure zero. Smooth positive closed κ satisfies the background hypotheses. This checks the application on a closed surface without borrowing original-dimensional subsolution attainment.

On the original-dimensional product, the supplied equivalence between the full genuine-subsolution threshold and exact clipped normalization limits is retained as a premise. Likewise, the supplied equivalence of ρ with the supremum over ALL normalized smooth dd^c-closed tests is retained. Neither is replaced by a factor-restricted definition.

notes.text:
Use δ=dd^c=i∂bar∂/(2π). Let X=X0×Y with projections π0 and πY, and pull back all factor forms. Put N=m+k, C=binomial(N,m), V0=∫X0 h0^m>0, c0=CV0, H=h0+κ and μ=(h0^m/V0)∧κ^k.

The product is compact and connected. For a nonzero tangent vector (a,b), H((a,b),overline{(a,b)})=h0(a,bar a)+κ(b,bar b)>0, so H is positive. Factor dimensions give

H^N=C h0^m∧κ^k=c0μ.

Therefore ∫X H^N=c0 and μ is a smooth positive probability. For any smooth positive probability dV, R=μ/dV is smooth positive, and compactness gives 0<a=min R≤R≤A=max R<∞.

Let w be a genuine canonical bounded h0-psh function. Its pullback u=π0*w is a genuine canonical bounded H-psh function because

H+δu=(h0+δw)+κ≥0.

In product coordinates this is the original canonical quasi-psh function, constant in the other variables. Projection is a submersion and introduces no reassignment of values on fibers.

Canonical bounded local products satisfy

(H+δu)^N=C(h0+δw)^m∧κ^k.

The binomial expansion is valid for these products. Terms with more than m horizontal or k vertical factors vanish; the total degree N forces precisely m horizontal and k vertical factors. Neither closedness of h0 nor a Stokes formula for h0 is used. Consequently,

∫X(H+δu)^N=C∫X0(h0+δw)^m.

If v_minus(h0)=0, choose bounded canonical admissible wj whose base masses tend to zero. Their pullbacks are competitors for the ORIGINAL bounded-potential infimum on X with masses tending to zero. Positivity of the measures gives the opposite inequality v_minus(H)≥0. Thus v_minus(H)=0.

In this zero-infimum setting, the original dimension requirement is automatic. A zero-dimensional connected base has mass one, and on a compact curve bounded Stokes gives the constant mass V0. Therefore v_minus(h0)=0 requires m≥2 here, and k≥2 implies N≥4.

This proves A conditionally on the specified base hypothesis. It does not identify a base with zero lower mass or reuse an absent prior elliptic-factor proof. No fixed-density Gauduchon volume is substituted for the bounded-potential infimum.

First suppose g is bounded. The checked bounded normalization theorem on (Y,κ) gives a continuous κ-psh v and c>0 such that

(κ+δv)^k=cgκ^k.

Normalize sup v=0. Bounded closed Stokes gives ∫(κ+δv)^k=∫κ^k=1, hence c=1/G. This covers zeros in g and k=2.

For u=πY*v, bounded product algebra gives

(H+δu)^N=C h0^m∧(κ+δv)^k
=(C/G)h0^m∧gκ^k=(c0/G)Rg dV.

The product density relative to H^N=c0R dV is g/c0, which satisfies the checked bounded-normalization hypotheses. Uniqueness of the continuous-equation scalar therefore identifies

c_H(Rg)=c0/G.

No potential uniqueness is used. The base contributes its actual h0^m; u=0 already solves the constant-one base equation, so no additional base normalization is hidden.

Now let g∈L¹(κ^k) be nonnegative and nonzero. F=Rg belongs to L¹(dV), since ∫X F dV=G. Use the EXACT ORIGINAL clips

Fj=min(Rg,j), gj−=min(g,j/A), gj+=min(g,j/a).

Pointwise,

Rgj−≤Fj≤Rgj+.

For the left inequality, when g>j/A one has Rj/A≤j and ≤Rg. For the right inequality, when g>j/a one has Rj/a≥j. The other cases are immediate.

The full threshold is decreasing with its density: if F≤F′, every genuine subsolution for tF′dV is also a subsolution for tF dV, so b_H(F)≥b_H(F′). For a bounded nonzero density B, the supplied exact-clip characterization gives b_H(B)=c_H(B), because its sufficiently large clips equal B. Using the bounded factor formula therefore yields

c0/∫gj+κ^k ≤ c_H(min(Rg,j)) ≤ c0/∫gj−κ^k.

Both denominators increase to G. Thus the exact original clip scalars converge to c0/G, and the supplied full threshold characterization gives

b_H(Rg)=c0/G.

This evaluates the unrestricted subsolution threshold, without restricting the dual test family.

The closed-factor threshold is proved directly, including on a surface. For any genuine κ-psh w, normalize sup w=0 and put wj=max(w,−j). Bounded closed Stokes gives ∫(κ+δwj)^k=1. MA_κ^ext(v)=(g/G)κ^k,

notes.text:
Use n1–n3. Given nonzero g≥0 in L¹(κ^k), let G=∫gκ^k and take the genuine canonical factor solution v constructed in n3, with sup v=0, MA_κ^ext(v)=(g/G)κ^k and actual mass one.

Specify the existence class by

P_E={πY*w : w∈E(Y,κ), supY w=0},
E(Y,κ)={w genuine canonical κ-psh : ∫Y MA_κ^ext(w)=1}.

Adding constants gives the corresponding unnormalized class. Existence is proved in P_E; no assertion is made that all H solutions are pullbacks.

Set u=πY*v. Projection preserves the local canonical quasi-psh representative, including −∞ values on pole fibers, and

H+δu=h0+πY*(κ+δv)≥0.

For every positive integer j,

vj=max(v,−j), uj=max(u,−j)=πY*vj.

Bounded product algebra gives

(H+δuj)^N=C h0^m∧πY*(κ+δvj)^k.

Multiplying by 1_{u>−j}=πY*1_{v>−j}, and putting νj=1_{v>−j}(κ+δvj)^k, gives the exact finite-level identity

1_{u>−j}(H+δuj)^N=C h0^m∧πY*νj.                 (1)

For a nonnegative Borel test function Φ on X, the right side means

C∫Y[∫X0 Φ(x,y)h0^m(x)]dνj(y).

The defining measures νj increase to MA_κ^ext(v). Monotone convergence in this integral therefore passes (1) through the defining construction and proves

MA_H^ext(πY*v)=C h0^m∧πY*MA_κ^ext(v).            (2)

This is passage through exact truncations of one fixed potential. It is not passage from arbitrary potential approximations and needs no unproved capacity compactness.

Substituting the factor equation and n3’s full threshold yields

MA_H^ext(u)=(C/G)h0^m∧gκ^k
=(c0/G)Rg dV=b_H(Rg)Rg dV.

The total mass is CV0=c0<∞. This proves C for every stated L¹ g, including k=2.

The same finite-level argument works for any genuine canonical κ-psh w. Closed bounded Stokes bounds its extended mass by one, and (2) gives

∫X MA_H^ext(πY*w)=c0∫Y MA_κ^ext(w).

Thus, among canonical pullbacks, actual product mass c0 is equivalent to actual factor mass one. The full-mass class among pullbacks is precisely πY*E(Y,κ).

Neither this definition nor the proof supplies generic smaller-background membership, stretching, compactness of general potentials, or whole-family unbounded-potential uniqueness.

ρ_H(p)=b_H(|p|^N)^(-1/N)=sup_T∫X|p|k_T dV,

where the supremum includes every smooth positive (N−1,N−1) form T with δT=0, ∫H∧T=1, T=γ^(N−1), and k_T=(γ^N/dV)^((N−1)/N). The zero convention is ρ_H(0)=0. The supplied equivalence is used with its entire test family.

For real or complex ξ∈L^N(Y,κ^k), define Jξ=R^(1/N)πY*ξ. This is linear over the chosen field. Since R dV=μ and the horizontal probability h0^m/V0 has integral one,

∫X|Jξ|^N dV=∫Y|ξ|^Nκ^k.

Thus ||Jξ||_N=||ξ||_N. If ξ≠0, apply n3 with g=|ξ|^N to obtain

ρ_H(Jξ)=(∫Y|ξ|^Nκ^k/c0)^(1/N)
=c0^(-1/N)||ξ||_N.                                (3)

For ξ=0 this follows from the convention. Applying (3) to ξ−η proves it for all real or complex differences. Hence

||Jξ||_N+ρ_H(Jξ)=(1+c0^(-1/N))||ξ||_N.

For closedness, suppose Jξj converges to p in D_H norm. This identity makes ξj Cauchy in L^N(Y); let ξ be its limit. Formula (3) for differences gives convergence Jξj→Jξ in D_H norm, and the L^N parts imply p=Jξ. Therefore image(J) is closed in D_H.

The full supremum formula implies lattice monotonicity: |p|≤|q| almost everywhere gives ρ_H(p)≤ρ_H(q), since every k_T is nonnegative. The actual amplitude set satisfies

{|Jξ|>K}={R|ξ|^N>K^N}⊂πY^*{|ξ|^N>K^N/A}.

Consequently,

|Jξ|1_{|Jξ|>K}≤J(|ξ|1_{|ξ|^N>K^N/A}),

and lattice monotonicity followed by (3) gives

ρ_H(Jξ1_{|Jξ|>K})
≤(∫_{|ξ|^N>K^N/A}|ξ|^Nκ^k/c0)^(1/N)→0.          (4)

The L^N norm of that actual tail is bounded by the same factor integral without c0, also tending to zero. The roots Jξ1_{|Jξ|≤K} are bounded and have finite ρ by lattice monotonicity. They converge to Jξ in exactly ||·||_N+ρ_H(·). Therefore image(J)⊂D_H^0.

notes.text:
Let Y=P^k, k≥2, and use exactly δ=i∂bar∂/(2π). The normalized Fubini–Study form κ has local potential log(1+Σ|zi|²). Fix 0<α<1 and define

ψ=log[(Σ_{i=1}^k|Zi|²)/(Σ_{i=0}^k|Zi|²)],
χ(x)=1−(1−x)^α for x≤0, and vα=χ(ψ).

The expression for ψ is homogeneous-scale invariant, is ≤0, is smooth off o=[1:0:…:0], and has canonical value −∞ at o. Locally,

κ+δψ=δlog(Σ_{i≥1}|Zi/Zj|²)≥0.

Thus ψ is the genuine canonical κ-psh logarithmic-pole function. Since χ′>0, χ″>0 and χ′≤α<1, the exact smooth chain rule gives

κ+δχ(ψ)=(1−χ′)κ+χ′(κ+δψ)+χ″dψ∧d^cψ≥0,

where d^c=i(bar∂−∂)/(4π) and dψ∧d^cψ=(i/(2π))∂ψ∧bar∂ψ. This fixes the rank-one coefficient.

For canonical extension, put ψL=max(ψ,−L). Convex composition with χ preserves κ-psh functions: choose a smooth local potential P for κ and represent χ as the supremum of supporting affine functions ax+b with 0<a≤α<1. Then

P+aψL+b=a(P+ψL)+(1−a)P+b

is psh. Their supremum equals the already upper-semicontinuous, locally bounded-above function P+χ(ψL), so it is psh. The functions χ(ψL) decrease to vα with value −∞ at o. Its local growth is O(1+|log|z|²|^α), which is integrable, and it is finite off o. This gives the genuine canonical representative. Its supremum is zero on {Z0=0}.

Every infinity chart is nonsingular. On any chart Zj=1 with j≥1, let Sj=1+Σ_{i≥1,i≠j}|Zi/Zj|² and w0=Z0/Zj. Then

ψ=−log(1+|w0|²/Sj).

Since Sj>0, this and vα are smooth throughout the chart, including w0=0. These charts cover all infinity and every point except o.

On Z0=1, put t=Σ|zi|²>0 and

ψ=log(t/(1+t)), s=1−ψ=1+log((1+t)/t),
B=αs^(α−1), D=α(1−α)s^(α−2).

The local potential of κ+δvα is Φ(t)=log(1+t)+1−s^α. A radial complex Hessian has eigenvalues Φ′ in k−1 tangential directions and Φ′+tΦ″ radially. The corresponding κ eigenvalues are 1/(1+t) and 1/(1+t)². Direct differentiation, using s′=−1/[t(1+t)], gives

tΦ′=W(t)=(t+B)/(1+t),
B′=D/[t(1+t)],
Φ′+tΦ″=W′=(1−B+D/t)/(1+t)².

Therefore the exact relative eigenvalues and density are

λtan=1+B/t, λrad=1−B+D/t,
qα(t)=(1+B/t)^(k−1)(1−B+D/t).                    (5)

They are positive because B≤α<1 and D>0. At infinity qα→1−α, consistent with smooth extension. Its value at o can be assigned arbitrarily, for example zero, as a measurable density.

The differential normalization is checked explicitly. In this convention,

κ^k=(k!/π^k)(1+t)^(−k−1)dλ_{2k}.

The Euclidean shell is [π^k/(k−1)!]t^(k−1)dt. Hence the exact normalized radial volume is

k t^(k−1)/(1+t)^(k+1)dt=d((t/(1+t))^k),

whose integral is one. Combining with (5) gives

qα(t)k t^(k−1)/(1+t)^(k+1)dt
=kW^(k−1)W′dt=d(W^k).                            (6)

As t→0, B→0 and W→0. As t→∞, B→α and W→1. Thus the smooth density on the punctured affine chart integrates to one. The infinity hyperplane has zero measure for its smooth local density.

Actual extended mass follows from the defining truncations. For vj=max(vα,−j), its cutoff radius is determined by

sj=(j+1)^(1/α), tj=1/(exp(sj−1)−1).

The strict superlevel {vα>−j} is {t>tj} in the affine chart and includes infinity. Locality of bounded canonical products makes the finite-level measure exactly 1_{t>tj}qακ^k. Its total mass, by (6), is 1−W(tj)^k. These measures increase, tj→0 and W(tj)→0. Their defining limit is therefore

MA_κ^ext(vα)=qακ^k,

of actual mass one. The pole belongs to none of the strict superlevels, so there is no atom there. Thus vα∈E(Y,κ). By n4, its canonical product pullback solves the exact H equation for qα and has mass c0. This example’s factor-mass calculation does not rely on an external existence theorem.

Write L=log(1/t) and β=k(1−α)>0. As t→0, s∼L, B/t→∞ and D/t dominates 1−B. Thus

qα(t)∼α^k(1−α)t^(−k)L^(−β−1).                   (7)

Its radial measure is comparable to t^(−1)L^(−β−1)dt, which is integrable. All other charts are smooth, so qα∈L¹. For p>1, the radial integrand for qα^p is comparable to

t^(k−1−kp)L^(−p(β+1))dt.

Substitution t=exp(−L) gives exp(k(p−1)L)L^(−p(β+1))dL, whose integral diverges. Therefore qα belongs to no L^p, p>1.

These are actual holomorphic transition maps. The action of g is c↦qc, so quotient bundle charts are U_ij×(C*/q^Z). Their logarithmic fibre coordinate belongs to E=C/(2πZ+2πiZ). Logarithms of transition functions give translations in E independent of the chosen logarithm. On U_00 the coordinates are exactly x=z1/z0, y=w1/w0, ζ=log(w0/z0).

The action is free: [z:q^m w]=[z:w], with z,w≠0, forces the projective scalar to be 1 and then q^m=1. It is properly discontinuous because t(g^m P)=t(P)+4πm: compact subsets of Ω have bounded t and meet only finitely many translates. Small open sets with disjoint translates give quotient manifold charts. Thus X0 is a smooth complex threefold. Ω is connected as the image of (C²∖{0})×(C²∖{0}), hence X0 is connected. Every quotient point has a representative z=Z, w=e^{t/2}W with Z,W∈S³ and 0≤t≤4π. The image of this compact parameter set covers X0, proving compactness.

On U_00,
t=ζ+barζ+log(1+|y|²)−log(1+|x|²),

Use the quotient geometry from n1. The prescribed Bδ is globally smooth after extension by zero: the base cutoffs are compactly supported, and the smooth density p vanishes with all derivatives at its support boundary. Its ζ-support lies in an injective logarithmic neighbourhood. It is semipositive. On a fixed compact neighbourhood of these supports, σ_ζ≤Kω, so
0≤Bδ≤K||p||∞δ^{-2}ω.
Every normalized positive test therefore satisfies ∫BδΘ≤K||p||∞δ^{-2}. Thus Cδ is finite. Its test family is nonempty by Θ* from n1.

We first reconstruct the compactness needed below. On a connected compact complex manifold, genuine quasi-psh functions u_j with dd^c u_j≥−h for fixed smooth Hermitian h and sup u_j=0 have an L1-convergent subsequence. Choose finitely many relatively compact connected coordinate balls, with smaller cores covering the manifold. On each choose a bounded quadratic correction ρ with dd^cρ≥h. Then u_j+ρ is genuine psh. Subtracting a fixed upper bound for ρ gives a nonpositive subharmonic function w_j.

The maxima of u_j are attained. Pass to a subsequence whose maximum points converge to p. In a chart about p, w_j at those points has a uniform lower bound. Submean on fixed-radius balls centred there bounds ∫(−w_j); a fixed smaller ball about p lies in these balls for all sufficiently large j. This supplies an initial uniform L1 bound.

To propagate it, in a connected coordinate domain let S be the points having neighbourhoods with uniformly bounded ∫(−w_j). S is open. If x is in its relative closure, choose B(x,4r) inside the domain and a fixed ball A⊂S∩B(x,r/4). The bound on A supplies points a_j∈A with w_j(a_j)≥−M for one fixed finite M. Submean on B(a_j,r) bounds its integral of −w_j. Since B(x,r/2)⊂B(a_j,r), x∈S. Thus S is relatively closed and equals the connected coordinate domain. Finite coverings then bound every compact subset. Across overlapping charts, bounded corrections and bounded coordinate Jacobians on a smaller overlap transfer these bounds. The intersection graph of a connected finite coordinate cover is connected, so they propagate across the cover. The smaller cores give a global L1 bound. The permitted local psh compactness theorem, followed by finite diagonal extraction, gives local and global L1 convergence. Limits patch as distributions, and uniqueness of canonical psh representatives after smooth correction makes the limit genuine. This proves the required global normalized compactness.

Suppose δ_j→0 and C_{δ_j}≤M. Put κ=1/(M+1). For EVERY smooth strictly positive dd^c-closed test Θ, normalization by ∫ωΘ gives
∫(ω−κB_{δ_j})Θ≥(1−κM)∫ωΘ>0.
Lamari's permitted nonclosed-form criterion yields real distributions u_j with
ω+dd^c u_j≥κB_{δ_j}.
Local quadratic corrections and the permitted representative theorem make these genuine quasi-psh functions. Subtract their finite suprema. Since dd^c u_j≥−ω, the compactness proof applies. Pass to u_j→u in L1.

The ordinary approximate-identity calculation in ζ gives
B_{δ_j}→χ0(x)χ0(y)[D_U],
where D_U={ζ=0} in the product chart; its normalization is ∫pσ_ζ=1. The base cutoffs permit extension by zero. Distributional limits preserve positivity, hence
T=ω+dd^c u≥κχ0(x)χ0(y)[D_U].
Near |x|,|y|<1/2 and ζ=0 this implies T≥κ[D_U].

On each coordinate ball choose ρ=M|z|² with dd^cρ≥ω. The current R=dd^c(u+ρ) is CLOSED and positive and dominates κ[D_U] near that local divisor. Its geometric Lelong number there is at least κ. In the geometric normalization a regular integration-current point has number 1: for a flat complex two-plane, the integral of (σ1+σ2)² over a radius-r ball is r^4. On overlaps the corrected currents differ by a smooth form, whose ball integral is O(r^6) and whose geometric Lelong contribution after division by r^4 is zero. Thus their numbers define one intrinsic function ν_u. Siu applies locally to these closed positive currents of bidimension (2,2). Consequently A={ν_u≥κ/2} is a global closed analytic subset of dimension at most 2 containing the indicated open part of D_U. No Siu theorem for a nonclosed current has been used.

Lift A through the quotient covering to an analytic subset Ã⊂Ω. The hypersurface D0={w0=z0}∩Ω is connected: it is P2 with the two points where z=0 or w=0 removed. Since Ã∩D0 is analytic in that connected surface and contains a nonempty open subset, the identity principle gives D0⊂Ã. Quotient invariance gives Dm={w0=q^m z0}∩Ω⊂Ã for every integer m.

At P=[0:1:0:1]∈Ω use a=z0/z1, b=w0/z1 and r=w1/z1 near (0,0,1). Each Dm is b=q^m a. A local holomorphic defining function F of Ã has expansion F(a,b,r)=Σf_ij(r)a^i b^j. Vanishing on Dm gives, for every degree k and integer m,
Σ_{i+j=k}f_ij(r)q^{mj}=0.
For each r this is a polynomial in q^m with infinitely many distinct roots. All its coefficients vanish. Every f_ij is therefore identically zero. Every local defining function vanishes identically, so Ã has interior near P, contradicting dimension at most 2.

A bounded subsequence of Cδ as δ→0 is impossible; hence Cδ→∞. This proves all of I for every prescribed p and χ0, including finiteness against all tests and the complete concentration implication. No quantitative lower divergence rate is claimed.
